title: Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would create offences for people over 18 who misrepresent their age online to minors to encourage a physical meeting or commit another offence.
The meeting offence would carry five years’ imprisonment, while misrepresentation intended to facilitate another offence would carry eight years, with additional rules about evidence.
The provisions would extend to fictitious recipients used in undercover operations and include defences concerning age belief and reasonable conduct by specified officers performing their duties.
changes: Encouraging a meeting with either the sender or another person would be covered.
A recipient’s represented age could establish the sender’s belief unless contrary evidence was provided.
A defendant could raise a belief that the recipient was not under 18, with its reasonableness considered.
summary.affected: Online message senders over 18, minors, and law enforcement, intelligence and security officers are affected.

speeches.speaker: Nick Xenophon
speeches.brief: The speaker moved to introduce the Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013, which creates new offences for misrepresenting age to minors online under the Criminal Code Act 1995. The bill was agreed to and read a first time.

speeches.speaker: Jacinta Collins
speeches.brief: The order of general business was set to consider first the Health Insurance Amendment (Medicare Funding for Certain Types of Abortion) Bill 2013, then the Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013. The motion was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: Anne McEwen
speeches.brief: The committee reports listed under order of business items 8 and 10 were tabled, and the Publications Committee's 26th report was adopted.
